processing: Little is documented for this location; raw pu-erh is normally pan-fired, rolled, sun-dried and then sold loose or pressed.
harvest_season: Not documented for this location; in Yiwu generally, spring is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Typical of Yiwu raw tea: long, dark-green large leaves, usually pressed.
appearance_liquor: Typical of young Yiwu raw tea: clear golden yellow.
appearance_wet: Typical of large-leaf raw tea: supple, olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: No reliable notes exist for this location; Yiwu teas in general are known for a soft, sweet liquor with gentle bitterness.

brewing.notes: Brew as you would other young Yiwu raw tea: very hot water and short steeps at first.

vintage_note: As usual for raw pu-erh it would be sold by harvest year, with spring lots most valued. Given the forest rules, supply under this name is small and irregular, and no vintage pattern is documented.
description:
Tongqinghe is a tea location named in Xishuangbanna's state forest, grouped in the market with the Yiwu area. It is known mainly for that status rather than for any described flavour.

Nothing specific is recorded about how its leaf is processed. The general raw pu-erh pattern applies: pan-firing, rolling, sun-drying and optional pressing.

Taste notes for Tongqinghe itself are missing, so anything here is class-level. Yiwu teas tend towards softness and sweetness, and it makes sense to start there when brewing.

Be sceptical of the name on a wrapper. Authorities have acted against illegal picking and planting in such forests, and a rare forest name is easy to print. Ask how the leaf was sourced.
history: Little is documented about Tongqinghe as a tea. A report on Yunnan spring prices names it among state-forest locations left out of the price index, as Xishuangbanna agencies were pursuing illegal picking and planting in those forests. Who first sold tea under this name, and when, is not recorded.
